# Bellmer La Poupée

"La Poupée" (French for "the doll") refers to a series of surrealistic dolls created by German artist Hans Bellmer (1902-1975) in the 1930s . These life-sized articulated figures, constructed with moveable parts, were photographed in various disturbing configurations and became iconic works of Surrealist art . The project began as a form of protest against Nazi ideology and evolved into a profound exploration of sexuality, identity, and the human form .

## 1. Background and Creation

### 1.1 Hans Bellmer's Early Life

Hans Bellmer was born in Katowice, Silesia (now Poland) in 1902 . He moved to Germany in 1911 and studied engineering at the Berlin Technische Hochschule from 1922 to 1924 . While there, he also studied perspective with George Grosz and established contact with Dada artists . After his education, he worked as a typographer in the advertising industry until 1933 .

Bellmer's artistic development was influenced by his exposure to various artistic movements. Through his interest in the Berlin Dada group, he met artists such as Georg Grosz, Helmut Herzfield (later known as John Heartfield), and Rudolf Schlichter . In the late 1920s, he saw photographs of mannequins made by Bauhaus artists Umbo (Otto Maximilian Umbehr) and Xanti Schawinsky, as well as works by Paul Citroen and Werner Rohde .

### 1.2 The Inspiration for La Poupée

Bellmer's inspiration for La Poupée came from multiple sources. He was influenced by reading the published letters of Austrian poet and playwright Oskar Kokoschka, who had created a life-sized doll of his former lover . Additionally, he attended a performance of Jacques Offenbach's "Tales of Hoffman" in which a man falls in love with an automaton . In 1932, he was further inspired by the opera "The Tales of Hoffmann," and the following year collaborated on a production of Hoffmann's "The Sandman," both works featuring female automatons .

The political climate in Germany also played a crucial role in the creation of La Poupée. When Adolf Hitler seized power on January 30, 1933, Bellmer decided he would no longer take on paid work for the advertising industry . He regarded every form of "useful" work as a contribution to the efficient functioning of the state and the increase of Hitler's power . In response, he began work on La Poupée, which he described as "a compensation for a life that has become impossible" .

### 1.3 The Construction Process

Bellmer began constructing his first doll in 1933 with the help of his wife Margarete, his brother Fritz, and his niece Ursula . The first doll stood approximately 135 cm (53 inches) tall and was constructed with a wood-and-metal skeleton covered with plaster and papier-mâché . The doll's body parts could be disassembled and rearranged into various poses .

The construction process was labor-intensive. Bellmer described the experience: "It was worth all my obsessive efforts when, amid the smell of glue and wet plaster, the essence of all that is impressive would take shape and become a real object to be possessed" . The doll was designed with ball-and-socket joints that allowed for endless configurations, enabling Bellmer to position it in increasingly disturbing and surreal poses .

In 1935, Bellmer constructed a second doll with even more sophisticated ball-and-socket joints that made it even more flexible . He described the new possibilities: "Thanks to a single ball-and-socket joint it was possible to expand the imagination in a direction that was self-evidently even more disturbing" .

## 2. The Dolls and Their Characteristics

### 2.1 Physical Construction

The dolls were meticulously crafted with great attention to detail. The materials used included wood for the skeleton, metal for the joints, plaster for the body, and papier-mâché for additional forms . The dolls had realistic features including painted faces, hair, and sometimes clothing . Some versions had glass eyes .

The dolls were designed to be completely articulated, allowing Bellmer to manipulate them into various positions. This articulation was crucial to his artistic vision, as it enabled him to create photographs that explored the boundaries of human anatomy and movement . The dolls could be posed in ways that suggested dismemberment, contortion, or impossible physical configurations .

### 2.2 Photographic Staging

Bellmer created a series of photographs of the dolls in carefully staged settings. These photographs were often taken in domestic interiors, including bedrooms and living rooms . The dolls were sometimes shown with sexualized props including black veils, lacy undergarments, or flowers . In other photographs, the dolls appeared as piles of dismembered parts .

The staging of the photographs was deliberate and meaningful. The claustrophobic, domestic settings in which Bellmer placed the doll were completely at odds with the image of the home as a place of order and virtue that was being promoted by the German government . This created a subversive commentary on Nazi ideals of domestic harmony and racial purity .

### 2.3 The Book "Die Puppe"

In 1934, Bellmer anonymously published a book titled "Die Puppe" (The Doll) in Karlsruhe, Germany . The book contained 10 black-and-white photographs of the first doll arranged in a series of tableaux vivants (living pictures) . The photographs were printed as gelatin silver prints and mounted on yellow cardboard with text printed on pink paper .

The book was published in a limited edition, with some sources indicating only 100 copies were made . The photographs in the book showed the doll in various configurations, from fully assembled to partially disassembled . The book included an introduction titled "Memories of the Doll Theme" .

## 3. Reception and Cultural Impact

### 3.1 Surrealist Adoption

The surrealist movement quickly embraced Bellmer's work. In 1934, photographs of the doll appeared in the surrealist journal *Minotaure* with the title "Poupée: Variations sur le montage d'une mineure articulée" (Doll: Variations on the assembly of an articulated minor) . The surrealists, including André Breton, Paul Éluard, Henri Parisot, and Georges Hugnet, were immediately captivated by Bellmer's creation .

The surrealists saw in Bellmer's dolls a perfect embodiment of their exploration of the unconscious mind and the concept of the uncanny . The photographs connected with the Freudian concept of the "unheimlich" (uncanny or strangely familiar) . The surrealists recognized the dolls as powerful objects that challenged conventional notions of beauty, sexuality, and identity .

### 3.2 Nazi Condemnation

The Nazi regime had a drastically different reaction to Bellmer's work. His art was classified as "degenerate art" (entartete Kunst) . The sexualized and distorted images of the female form were seen as a direct challenge to Nazi ideals of Aryan physical perfection and moral purity .

Bellmer's decision to create art that was explicitly "useless" in a productive sense was itself a form of protest against the Nazi regime . By refusing to create art that supported the state or promoted Nazi ideology, he was engaging in a form of passive resistance . The hand-tinted versions of his photographs, which created a sense of diseased skin, were interpreted by art historian Therese Lichtenstein as a direct protest against the desire for perfection in Nazi "body culture" .

### 3.3 Critical Analysis

Scholars have interpreted Bellmer's work in various ways. Some view the dolls as a form of protest against Nazi ideology . Others see them as explorations of Bellmer's own psychological state, including his gender identity issues and sexual obsessions . The dolls have been analyzed as both political and personal statements .

Art historian Paul Ardenne described the doll as "this 'artificial girl', automaton but also sculpture, model for photography but also transitional object serving as enigmatic staging where the artist sometimes inserts himself" . He noted that the doll "plays clearly the role of an oppressive, stubborn figure" .

The dolls have also been analyzed in terms of their relationship to the female body. Some scholars argue that Bellmer's manipulation of the doll represents an attempt at control over the female form . However, others note that the doll's autonomy and the unexpected configurations it could take suggest a more complex relationship .

## 4. Legacy and Influence

### 4.1 Artistic Influence

Bellmer's influence on subsequent artists has been considerable. His work has inspired numerous artists including Salvador Dalí, André Masson, and Meret Oppenheim, who created dolls for the 1938 Surrealist exhibition in Paris . Later artists influenced by Bellmer include Frederick Sommer, Ralph Eugene Meatyard, and Cindy Sherman .

Bellmer's use of the doll as a artistic medium and his exploration of the human form through photography and sculpture have had a lasting impact on contemporary art . His work has been featured in numerous exhibitions, including the 1947 International Surrealist Exposition in Paris .

### 4.2 Literary and Cultural References

Bellmer's work has been referenced in literature and popular culture. The surrealist poet Paul Éluard wrote texts to accompany Bellmer's photographs in the book "Les Jeux de la Poupée" (The Games of the Doll), published in 1949 . This collaboration between visual art and poetry further cemented the dolls' place in surrealist culture.

The dolls have also appeared in various films and other media. A 2009 video work titled "Hans Bellmer, 'Les Jeux de la poupée', 1938-49" was created by Nicolas Valode and Pauline Cathala . The dolls continue to be a source of inspiration for artists working in photography, sculpture, and performance art .

### 4.3 Museum Collections

Several museums around the world have Bellmer's dolls and related works in their collections. The Centre Pompidou in Paris has multiple versions of "La Poupée" including both photographic works and the actual doll . The Art Institute of Chicago has a photograph titled "The Doll (La Poupée)" from 1935 . The Reina Sofía Museum in Madrid has a gelatin silver print from 1934 .

The dolls are considered important works of 20th-century art and are studied for their technical innovation, artistic merit, and cultural significance . They are often included in exhibitions and scholarly discussions about surrealism, the body in art, and the relationship between art and politics .

## 5. Controversies and Criticisms

### 5.1 Sexual Content and Pedophilia

One of the most controversial aspects of Bellmer's work is its sexual content, particularly the focus on pubescent female figures . The dolls are explicitly sexualized, with some photographs showing them in suggestive poses wearing lingerie or other erotic clothing . This has led to accusations that Bellmer's work is pedophilic or exploitative .

Bellmer's biographer Peter Webb detected "intimations of rape" in one particularly disturbing photograph of the doll partly lying, partly seated on a rumpled bed, half-dressed in a man's trousers with the belt and fly provocatively open . This interpretation highlights the complex and troubling nature of Bellmer's imagery .

### 5.2 Questions of Authorship

The question of authorship has also been raised in connection with Bellmer's work. Some scholars have suggested that his wife Margarete and his niece Ursula may have played a more significant role in the creation of the dolls than is generally acknowledged . Ursula, in particular, was involved in the construction process and was the one who showed the photographs to André Breton when she went to Paris in 1934 .

The anonymous publication of "Die Puppe" has also led to speculation about whether Bellmer was the sole creator of the work . While Bellmer is generally credited as the primary artist, the collaborative nature of the project raises questions about authorship and artistic credit .

### 5.3 Political Interpretations

The political interpretation of Bellmer's work has been debated by scholars. While some view the dolls as a form of resistance against Nazi ideology , others argue that this interpretation may be overly simplistic. The complex and ambiguous nature of the work allows for multiple readings .

Some scholars have suggested that Bellmer's work can be read as expressing his own gender identity issues, engaging with the alternative realities of surrealism, and commenting on Nazi Germany's notions of the "perfect" versus the degenerate body . This multi-layered interpretation suggests that the work operates on multiple levels simultaneously .

## 6. Conclusion

"Bellmer La Poupée" represents one of the most significant and controversial artistic projects of the 20th century. Hans Bellmer's dolls challenged conventional notions of art, sexuality, and identity while serving as a form of protest against the political and social climate of Nazi Germany . The dolls' surreal and disturbing imagery continues to provoke strong reactions and inspire new interpretations .

The technical innovation of the articulated dolls, combined with Bellmer's photographic staging and the surrealist movement's adoption of the work, established "La Poupée" as an important contribution to 20th-century art . The dolls have influenced countless artists and continue to be studied for their artistic merit, technical innovation, and cultural significance .

However, the work's controversial nature, particularly its sexual content and ambiguous political messages, ensures that it remains a subject of debate and interpretation . As art historian Paul Ardenne noted, the doll "is at the heart of an eminently transgressive work" that continues to challenge viewers and inspire new artistic responses .

The legacy of "Bellmer La Poupée" extends beyond the realm of art into broader discussions about the body, identity, and the relationship between art and power. The dolls stand as powerful symbols that continue to resonate in contemporary discussions about gender, sexuality, and the boundaries of artistic expression .

Description

A [first edition](https://www.sothebys.com/en/buy/luxury/books-&-manuscripts/book/first-edition?locale=en) of _La Poupée_ by [Hans Bellmer](https://www.sothebys.com/en/search?query=Hans%20Bellmer&tab=objects&sortBy=bsp_dotcom_prod_en).

*   Hans Bellmer (German).
*   Paris: GLM [Guy Lévis-Mano], 1936.
*   44 pages.
*   Number 76 of 100 copies with 5 hors commerce, this being one of 80 copies on papier rose.
*   10 mounted gelatin silver photographs.
*   Text translated by Robert Valençay.
*   Pink wrappers, peach printed folding cover with titles on upper side in black, in a custom box by Devauchelle.

_La Poupée_ evolved out of a series of events in Hans Bellmer’s personal life: his cousin, Ursula Naguschewski, moving from Kassel to Berlin in 1932; an encounter with renowned dollmaker Lotte Pritzel and his attendance of a performance of Jacques Offenbach’s Tales of Hoffmann, in which the protagonist falls in love with an automaton; and his mother shipping him his old toys. Bellmer constructed several dolls, the first dating from 1933, which he assembled and photographed in strange and disquieting configurations. Ten of these photographs were published in Germany as _Die Puppe_ (1934). It was Bellmer’s cousin Ursula who, while studying at the Sorbonne in 1934, apparently first brought Bellmer’s photographs to the attention of André Breton in Paris. In 1934, the Surrealist journal Minotaure published a portfolio of these images, and in 1936, one was published in an issue of Cahiers d’art devoted to the Surrealist object. Guy Levis Manos published this expanded French Edition with an introduction by Bellmer, translated by Robert Valencay. In February 1938, Bellmer left Berlin for Paris.

Die Puppe (La muñeca)
=====================

[Bellmer, Hans](https://www.museoreinasofia.es/colecciones/artista/bellmer-hans)

Técnica Gelatinobromuro de plata sobre papel

Dimensiones Soporte: 47 x 71 cm

Año de ingreso 2002

Número de registro AD02453

Fecha
1934 / Copia de época

Hans Bellmer fue un artista vinculado al movimiento surrealista, formado en el Berlín de los años veinte bajo la influencia de las enseñanzas de George Grosz y de las lecturas de Karl Marx y Vladimir Lenin. Su proyecto inicial más relevante fue _Die Puppe_ (La muñeca), que comenzó en 1932 y continuó desarrollando durante varios años. Bellmer construyó una serie de piezas de maniquí con atributos femeninos que ensamblaba en una variedad de combinaciones y escenarios donde fotografiarla. Bellmer abordaba la construcción del cuerpo femenino como un juego lingüístico por el cual la asociación libre de unidades era capaz de despertar y desvelar significados profundos, ocultos en la psique. Las imágenes resultantes conectaban con el concepto freudiano de lo siniestro o lo extraño inquietante y cautivaron a los miembros del grupo surrealista. Esa conexión, junto a la calificación de la producción de Bellmer como «arte degenerado» en la Alemania nazi, impulsó la huida del artista a Francia. En 1934 se publicó una secuencia de sus fotografías en la revista _Minotaure_ bajo el título _La Poupée_. Un año después, en 1935, esta obra, con un encuadre más amplio, formó parte de la Exposición Surrealista celebrada en el Ateneo de Santa Cruz de Tenerife. En ese mismo año, Bellmer editaría el libro _Die Puppe_.

 Concha Calvo Salanova

細節

**BELLMER, Hans (1902-1975) - ÉLUARD, Paul (1895-1952).**_Les Jeux de la Poupée. Illustrés de textes par Paul Éluard_. Paris : les Éditions Premières, 1949.

 Célèbre ouvrage de Hans Bellmer "illustrés de textes par Paul Éluard", tel que paru. Au début des années 30, alors qu'il assiste à une représentation des _Contes d'Hoffmann_, Hans Bellmer est subjugué par le personnage d'Olympia, fille artificielle à laquelle le Marchand de sable a donné vie. En 1934, il fait paraître à compte d'auteur, un opuscule intitulé _Die Puppe_, recueil de 10 photographies d'une poupée de plâtre et de papier mâché, moulée sur une armature de plâtre et de papier. Au travers de cette publication, Bellmer incarne peut-être déjà ce "démon d'anatomiste" dont parlait Hoffmann, qui manipule sa "poupée articulée, destinée à servir toutes sortes d'essais diaboliques". La publication attire l'attention des Surréalistes parisiens, qui lui consacrent une double page dans le numéro de décembre 1934 de leur revue Minotaure. Bellmer travaille alors sur une seconde poupée, avec de nouveaux mécanismes et des "jointures à boules", qui permettent plus de liberté dans l'agencement de son corps, plus d'inventivité dans ces "jeux anatomiques". Paul Éluard planche également sur des textes censés accompagner une seconde publication de clichés de cette poupée. Comme l'indique la formulation du titre, le projet est de "renverser la hiérarchie traditionnelle des rapports texte/image, pour faire des poèmes d'Éluard des illustrations" des photographies (Han, 8), sur le modèle du _Facile_ de Man Ray, publié par GLM en 1935. 

 L'ouvrage est prêt dès 1939, et sa parution est annoncée en juin dans la revue _Messages_. La guerre interrompt le projet, et le livre ne paraît à Paris qu'en 1949, sous la direction d'hans Berggruen. Parr-Badger, I, 106-107 ; _Eros invaincu_, cat. 115 ; Hans Bellmer. Filipacchi, 1971, pp. 74 et 83 ; Ji-Yoon Han, "La Poupée de Bellmer : variations éditoriales sur le montage d'une série photographique", 2012 ; Rouquette, "Hans Bellmer, la femme et la poupée", in Cahiers Jungiens de psychanalyse, 117, pp. 17-23. 

**Édition originale**, tirage total à 142 exemplaires numérotés au tampon, tous sur vélin Crèvecœur du Marais, celui-ci un des 120 avec les 15 photographies, n° 53, non signé à la justification.

 In-4 (245 x 190 mm). Un tirage argentique coloré et découpé, répété sur la couverture et la page de titre, 15 tirages argentiques originaux de Hans Bellmer hors-texte, coloriés à la main (légère ondulation au plat supérieur et aux pages intérieures). Couverture rempliée noire de l'éditeur, premier plat à vignette photographique collée et bande typographique rose.

Informations détaillées
-----------------------

| Résumé | Oeuvre présentée par Quentin Bajac, commissaire de l’exposition "La subversion des images" qui se tient du 23 septembre 2009 au 11 janvier 2011 au Centre Pompidou, Galerie 2. Hans Bellmer a modelé une créature féminine artificielle nommée "La poupée" qu’il met en scène d’une façon sulfureuse, provocante pour ensuite la photographier. "Les jeux de la poupée" fait partie de la collection du Centre Pompidou, Musée national d’art moderne, Paris. Galerie 1. |

### Encounter

Hans Bellmer
============

### La poupée, 1933-1945

05 Mar 2006

![Image 1: A hyperrealistic sculpture featuring a female figure with a melancholic expression, short dark hair, and an elongated neck, sitting above a conjoined second set of legs, wearing black Mary Jane shoes with white socks](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/media/picture/69/f7/69f75aab7474e56e7f404e8b7776c15b/thumb_large.jpg)

 Related to [Un dimanche, une oeuvre](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/program/calendar/event/c9jz669)

[Back to calendar](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/program/calendar)

The event is over

*   [Overview](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/program/calendar/event/c7ox6d#en_bref)
|*   [Related events](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/program/calendar/event/c7ox6d#programmation_associee)

![Image 2: A hyperrealistic sculpture featuring a female figure with a melancholic expression, short dark hair, and an elongated neck, sitting above a conjoined second set of legs, wearing black Mary Jane shoes with white socks](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/media/picture/69/f7/69f75aab7474e56e7f404e8b7776c15b/thumb_large.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, La Poupée, 1933-1945

© ADAGP

_La Poupée_, 1932-1945

Par Paul Ardenne, théoricien et critique d'art, maître de conférences en histoire de l'art et esthétique à l'université d'Amiens.

En relation avec l'exposition Hans Bellmer.

![Image 3: A hyperrealistic sculpture featuring a female figure with a melancholic expression, short dark hair, and an elongated neck, sitting above a conjoined second set of legs, wearing black Mary Jane shoes with white socks](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/media/picture/69/f7/69f75aab7474e56e7f404e8b7776c15b/thumb_large.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, La Poupée, 1933-1945

© ADAGP

Hans Bellmer, _La Poupée_, 1934

Par Paul Ardenne, historien de l’art (Faculté des arts, Amiens)

Cette conférence accompagne l’exposition _Hans Bellmer, Anatomie du désir_, présentée au Centre Pompidou du 1er mars au 22 mai 2006.

Dans l’importante production de mannequins et de poupées artistiques qu’enregistre l’entre-deux-guerres, la _Poupée_ d’Hans Bellmer occupe une place singulière. Fascinant, énigmatique, immédiatement adopté par les surréalistes, l’objet fétiche que met au point Bellmer est d’abord un travail obstiné d’ingénieur, une reconstruction physique particulièrement élaborée. Plus encore : cette « fille artificielle », automate mais également sculpture, modèle pour la photographie mais aussi objet transitionnel servant d’énigmatiques mises en scène où l’artiste s’insinue à l’occasion, joue clairement le rôle d’une figure oppressive, entêtante. Bellmer n’en use jamais gratuitement : la _Poupée_ ou l’expérience érotique du substitut torturé-torturant.

L’analyse de la _Poupée_, par extension, fournit l’occasion de réinterroger le rapport de Hans Bellmer au corps féminin représenté. Un corps magnétique, violenté mais plus autonome pourtant que ne le laissent imaginer les mises en scène de soumission que lui inflige l’artiste avec une rare intensité sadique.

La scène bellmérienne, celle de l’éternel féminin obsessionnel, indispensable et indomptable, pourrait bien être en bout de course l’aveu d’une tentative malheureuse, celle de la domination. Il n'y a pas extorsion totale du corps de la femme, serait-il réduit à la figure indéfiniment manipulable d’une _Poupée_ servile et de ses avatars ultérieurs couchés sur le papier.

Le « principe de perversion » (Pierre Dourthe) actif chez Hans Bellmer n’atteint que partiellement son but, la mise à disposition de la figure, et son aliénation. Restent la mécanique complexe des échanges, le désir en ses guerres interminables, l’amour même, en somme.

**Références bibliographiques**

Pierre Dourthe, _Bellmer_, _Le principe de perversion_, Jean-Pierre Faur, 1999.

Fabrice Flahutez, _Catalogue raisonné des estampes de Hans Bellmer_, Doubleff, 1999.

Céline Masson, _La fabrique de la Poupée chez Hans Bellmer_, L’Harmattan, 2000.

Sue Taylor, _Hans Bellmer. The Anatomy of Anxiety_, M.I.T. Press, 2000.

**Paul Ardenne**

Collaborateur, entre autres, de la revue _Art press_, Paul Ardenne est l’auteur de plusieurs ouvrages ayant trait à l’esthétique actuelle : _Art, l’âge contemporain_ (1997), _L’Art dans son moment politique_ (2000), _L’Image Corps_ (2001), _Un Art contextuel_ (2002), _Portraiturés_ (2003), outre diverses monographies d’architectes et un essai sur l’urbanité contemporaine, _Terre habitée_ (2005).

Prochaine publication : _Extrême - Esthétiques de la limite dépassée_ (Flammarion, sept. 2006).

The Doll (La Poupée)
--------------------

![Image 1: A work made of gelatin silver print overpainted with white gouache.](blob:http://localhost/fc94a919ccadf95281440efc2fb5d3d0)

 © 2017 Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York / ADAGP, Paris 
Image actions
-------------

*   ![Image 2: A work made of gelatin silver print overpainted with white gouache.](blob:http://localhost/fc94a919ccadf95281440efc2fb5d3d0)

 The Doll (La Poupée) 
Date:
-----

1935

Artist:
-------

Hans Bellmer

German, born Poland, 1902–1975

About this artwork
------------------

Hans Bellmer studied art and worked in advertising in the 1920s; when the Nazis seized power in 1933, he renounced useful employment as a kind of protest. Because of his background in commercial design, Bellmer was comfortable with procedures of studio photography, which he employed in his doll series, begun that same year: posing of the model, lighting, use of props, and extensive manual interventions (coloring, retouching, overpainting) on the final prints. The doll pictures do violence to a girlish body that seems nearly alive and somehow more real in feeling than the erotic magazine images manipulated by Bellmer’s contemporaries in the Surrealist movement. He made only a few prints at this remarkably large size, hand-coloring them and mounting them to stretchers as if they were paintings; quite improbably, some of these works were exhibited during World War II, when Bellmer lived in exile in southern France.

4.title: La Poupée [The Doll] by Hans Bellmer | National Galleries of Scotland
4.description: This photograph previously belonged to André Breton, the leader of the surrealist group, who was a great admirer of Bellmer's work. It shows Bellmer's second doll, made in 1935. Bellmer made several dolls, the first one in 1933, all of which had moveable parts that could be put together in many strange and disquieting combinations. Bellmer's photographs of his doll are carefully staged in both interior and exterior settings. They show how photography could further explore the eroticism of the doll and the obsessive desire that led to its creation.

### About this artwork

This photograph previously belonged to André Breton, the leader of the surrealist group, who was a great admirer of Bellmer's work. It shows Bellmer's second doll, made in 1935. Bellmer made several dolls, the first one in 1933, all of which had moveable parts that could be put together in many strange and disquieting combinations. Bellmer's photographs of his doll are carefully staged in both interior and exterior settings. They show how photography could further explore the eroticism of the doll and the obsessive desire that led to its creation.

**Updated before 2020**

### Surrealism

Surrealism was one of the most radical movements of the twentieth century. Founded by the poet André Breton in 1924 it was both a literary and artistic movement.

### Between the Covers: Surrealist Erotica

[Bottom](https://smarthistory.org/footer) Hans Bellmer, _The Doll/La Poupée_ ================================== by [Dr. Vanessa Rocco](https://smarthistory.org/author/dr-vanessa-rocco/ "Posts by Dr. Vanessa Rocco") [Artwork Details ![Image 17: Downward pointing arrow](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/themes/sh-new-theme/assets/images/red-down-arrow.svg)](https://smarthistory.org/collapseArtworkDetails) [![Image 18: Hans Bellmer, The Doll, 1935–37, gelatin silver print, 24.1 x 23.7 cm (The Museum of Modern Art, New Yo](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/W1siZiIsIjE2NTUwMyJdLFsicCIsImNvbnZlcnQiLCItcXVhbGl0eSA5MCAtcmVzaXplIDIwMDB4MjAwMFx1MDAzZSJdXQ-1-870x879.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/W1siZiIsIjE2NTUwMyJdLFsicCIsImNvbnZlcnQiLCItcXVhbGl0eSA5MCAtcmVzaXplIDIwMDB4MjAwMFx1MDAzZSJdXQ-1.jpg) Hans Bellmer, _The Doll_, 1935–37, gelatin silver print, 24.1 x 23.7 cm ([The Museum of Modern Art](https://www.moma.org/collection/works/43935), New York) The first time I encountered Hans Bellmer’s life-sized double-doll sculpture—at an exhibition I helped organize at the International Center of Photography in 2001—my feelings were a mix of shock, revulsion, and fascination. In _The Doll_ photo-series based on the sculpture, Hans Bellmer assembled and reassembled doll parts that he had constructed with his brother Fritz—also a trained engineer. Bellmer accentuated and duplicated their female sex organs, splaying them out on the floor as a still life before the viewer. Due to the nature of the work from this series, he is often pegged by scholars as a misogynist-leaning, female-objectifying artist—even to the extent of having alleged “pedophiliac” visual fantasies. [1] But Bellmer also provides a compelling example of the complexities of reading artwork retroactively. As scholars since the year 2000 have suggested with _The Doll_ and other photographs from the series, Bellmer also expressed his own gender-identity issues, engaged the alternative realities of [Surrealism](https://smarthistory.org/surrealism-origins-and-precursors/), and commented on Nazi Germany’s notions of the “perfect” versus the degenerate body. Bellmer was born in German-speaking Silesia but had been exposed to French Surrealism on trips to mid-1920s Paris, where he met the Italian artist much beloved by the Surrealists, [Giorgio De Chirico](https://smarthistory.org/de-chirico-soothsayers-recompense/), who often used mannequins as subjects for his paintings. Surrealist preoccupations with the uncanny melded with numerous highly personal events once the Bellmer family moved to Berlin in 1931. Together, these inspired the artist to construct his first life-sized doll in 1933—the same year Hitler took over as German Chancellor—which he could use as a subject for experimental photography. [2] That was followed by a more complex second doll in 1935 which was composed of a central ball joint that allowed for more flexibility and various appendages to be attached. While that opened up the object for Bellmer and kindled his desire to create various associations of gender and identity, it concurrently led to accusations of purposeful violence done to the doll’s “body” through implied amputations and sexualization. As Therese Lichtenstein explored in depth in her 2001 monograph _Behind Closed Doors: The Art of Hans Bellmer_, the convergence of three events between 1930–32 inspired him to construct the first doll. They included his mother sending him a box of his childhood toys—including broken dolls. He also had a Lolita-like fixation on his teenage cousin Ursula Naguschewski, newly arrived in Berlin where the Bellmer family had moved. And finally, he attended a local production of _The Tales of Hoffman_, a Jules Offenbach opera, where the first act centered on a “beautiful, lifelike doll Olympia.” [3] [![Image 19: Hans Bellmer, "Poupée: Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée (Doll: Variations on the Montage of an Articulated Minor)," Minotaure, number 6 (December 1934)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Minotaur-870x585.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Minotaur.jpg) Hans Bellmer, “Poupée: Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée (Doll: Variations on the Montage of an Articulated Minor),” _Minotaure_, number 6 (December 1934) ### The circulation of Bellmer’s _Dolls_ The artist took approximately 30 black-and-white photographs of the first doll, some of which were included in the 1934 book _Die Puppe_(_“Dolls_”)and which also appeared in the Surrealist publication _Minotaure_ in December of 1934. His cousin Ursula, then a Sorbonne student in Paris, had shown them to the Surrealist founder and poet André Breton at Bellmer’s request, and they caused “such a stir” that they were quickly published as the double-page spread above. [![Image 20: Hans Bellmer, La Poupée, 1935, hand colored gelatin silver print, 29.2 x 27.3 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/handcolored-300x321.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/handcolored.jpg) Hans Bellmer, _La Poupée_, 1935, hand colored gelatin silver print, 29.2 x 27.3 cm (private collection) Parts of that doll were then incorporated into the more monumental second doll in 1935, which was the subject of more than 100 photographs, including the images that have become “textbook” Bellmer such as _The Doll_ (_La Poupée_, 1935). This image was hand-tinted in candy-colored pastels, lovingly applied by Bellmer—an unusual practice when black-and-white photography was accepted as the default—with the parts adhered to a chair-caning surface. [4] In a way, it’s unfortunate that this image from the series has become one of the most widely disseminated examples of Bellmer’s work. As striking as it is, other images of the second doll speak more directly to the complexity of gender and political issues that the artist sorted out through these performative sculptural acts before photographing them, with the photographs then becoming his definitive works of art. A different photograph also entitled _The Doll_ (the repeated titles can become confounding) from 1936 shows how the ball joint of the more flexible second doll can be used to attach multiple legs. [![Image 21: Hans Bellmer, The Doll, 1936, hand-colored gelatin silver print, printed 1949, 13.7 x 13.7 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bellmer-trousers-870x859.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bellmer-trousers.jpg) Hans Bellmer, _The Doll_, 1936, hand-colored gelatin silver print, printed 1949, 13.7 x 13.7 cm (private collection) Bellmer therefore had more choices of garb here and chose to put one set of legs into men’s trousers and another set laid bare to show off girly patent-leather shoes. The artist was very forthcoming about his own lingering gender confusion, speculating that it may have been precipitated by his tyrannical, fascistic father who was obsessed with masculinity, underwhelmed by his sons’ lack of demonstration of it, and who eventually joined the Nazi Party. Bellmer described himself and his brother as children: “In fact, we were probably rather adorable, more like little girls than the formidable boys we would have preferred to be. Yet, it seemed to be more fitting than anything else to lure the brute out of his place in order to confuse him.” [5] And so it seems safe to presume that he often identified _himself_ directly with the doll. ### Rejecting Nazi “perfection” One of the most astonishing experiments with the doll parts is witnessed through a 1936 _Doll_ photograph, a hand-colored photographic print depicting a torso where a second set of legs replace the arms and head and which is dressed in red and clad in two sets of the black leather shoes: the type typically worn by young girls. Concurrently in the forest setting, an ominous and voyeuristic figure dressed in all black hovers behind a nearby tree, ready to pounce, with all the implied features of a strongly-built male. [![Image 22: Hans Bellmer, The Doll (La Poupée), 1936, hand-colored vintage gelatin silver print, 6 x 5.5 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Red-trousers-870x867.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Red-trousers.jpg) Hans Bellmer, _The Doll (La Poupée)_, 1936, hand-colored vintage gelatin silver print, 6 x 5.5 cm (private collection) Is this scene based on voyeuristic sexual fantasies? Or perhaps it refers to the suffocating environment of surveillance instituted by the Third Reich, a regime Bellmer protested, and as a result, refused to work or exhibit with publicly. He claimed _The Doll_ was a political artwork, but many viewers focused on the sexual content. Other hand-tinted images of the doll created a sense of diseased skin, which the art historian Therese Lichtenstein emphasizes was a protest against the desire for perfection in [Nazi](https://smarthistory.org/art-in-nazi-germany/) “body culture.” The persuasive combination of possibilities is precisely what complicates Bellmer’s arresting and disturbing works. ### Bellmer and Surrealism The interwar Nazi politics of Germany became so constricting for Bellmer that when his sickly wife died in 1938, he moved to Paris where he lived for the rest of his life. He was immediately embraced by the Surrealists there who included him in the [_International Exhibition of Surrealism_](https://smarthistory.org/surrealist-exhibitions/) in 1938, with its famed “Street of Mannequins.” Surrealist poet Paul Eluard wrote poems to accompany Bellmer’s second doll’s photographs in the book _Games of the Doll_, although it was not published until 1949. In the late 1940s Bellmer also collaborated with the author Georges Bataille, providing illustrations for his 1947 reprint of the novella _Story of the Eye._ Later in his career, he began additional “body-art” collaborations with his lover, the German writer and artist Unica Zürn. However, Zürn suffered deeply from her mental health issues, and died in 1970. The following year he was able to enjoy a definitive retrospective at the Centre national d’art contemporain, Paris, including an overview of his dolls. He died a few years later and was laid to rest in the illustrious Père Lachaise Cemetery in his beloved adopted city, where the artistic movement of Surrealism had always welcomed him with open arms. ### Artwork details Title The Doll/La Poupée Artist(s)[Hans Bellmer](https://smarthistory.org/artist/hans-bellmer/) Dates 1935–37 Places[Europe](https://smarthistory.org/place/europe/) / Central Europe / Germany Period, Culture, Style[Modernisms](https://smarthistory.org/period-culture-style/modernisms/) / [Surrealism](https://smarthistory.org/period-culture-style/modernisms/surrealism/) Artwork Type[Photograph](https://smarthistory.org/artwork-type/photograph/) / [Sculpture](https://smarthistory.org/artwork-type/sculpture/) Material Technique[Gelatin silver process](https://smarthistory.org/technique/gelatin-silver-process/) ### Footnotes [1] Ken Johnson, “[Desiring Machines: Hans Bellmer and Surrealist Strategies in Contemporary Photography](https://www.nytimes.com/2002/05/03/arts/art-review-desiring-machines-hans-bellmer-surrealist-strategies-contemporary.html),” _New York Times_ (May 3, 2002). This review shows that those assumptions about Bellmer lingered even after the turn of the millennium. [2] Freud’s essay regularly invoked dolls, mannequins, mirrors, and other doubles as examples of the “uncanny.” Sigmund Freud, “[The Uncanny](https://archive.org/details/freud-uncanny_001/mode/2up),” (1919), _The Standard Edition of the Complete Works of Sigmund Freud,_ volume 17, translated by James Strachey (London: The Hogarth Press, 1964), pp. 217–56. [3] Therese Lichtenstein, _Behind Closed Doors: The Art of Hans Bellmer_ (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001), p. 21. [4] For an example of such a textbook, see Mary Warner Marien, _Photography: A Cultural History,_ 5 th edition (London: Laurence King Publishing, 2021), p. 253. [5] Hans Bellmer, “Die Vater (The Father),” 1936, translated by Allen S. Weiss from the French, “Le Père,” which appeared as a prose poem in _Le Surréalism_, number 4 (Spring, 1958). See Lichtenstein, p. 177. ### Bibliography Yve-Alain Bois and Rosalind Krauss, _Formless: A User’s Guide_ (Princeton: Zone Books, 2000). Therese Lichtenstein, _Behind Closed Doors: The Art of Hans Bellmer_ (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001). Sue Taylor, _Hans Bellmer: The Anatomy of Anxiety_ (Cambridge: MIT Press, 2002). ### Important fundamentals [Surrealism, an introduction](https://smarthistory.org/surrealism-intro/) [Surrealism and Women](https://smarthistory.org/surrealism-and-women/) ### Cite this page Cite this page as: Dr. Vanessa Rocco, "Hans Bellmer, _The Doll/La Poupée_," in _Smarthistory_, February 7, 2024, accessed December 21, 2025, [https://smarthistory.org/hans-bellmer-the-doll/](https://smarthistory.org/hans-bellmer-the-doll/). Análisis
--------

Objet fétiche, placé au cœur d’une œuvre éminemment transgressive, essentiellement photographique et dessinée, la fameuse _Poupée_ grandeur nature de Hans Bellmer n’est pas loin d’être devenue une icône, ouvrant la voie à une réflexion très actuelle sur l’intégrité corporelle et l’identité sexuelle. De son temps, elle a œuvré comme une bombe, pulvérisant les catégories convenues : ni objet ni sculpture, elle se constitue en _organisme_ hybride, polymorphe, et en _instrument_ manipulable et transformable à l’infini. Et si elle peut être considérée comme un ultime avatar des mannequins, automates et robots produits en grande série dans l’Allemagne dévastée du tournant de la Grande Guerre, elle dépasse l’esprit de dérision et de satire sociale qui commandait cette vogue d’esprit dadaïste : à usage privé, répondant à une pulsion subjective (une nostalgie de l’enfance et de ses jeux, un abandon définitif à l’imagination érotique), elle est, au-delà de l’esprit de révolte contre l’ordre nazi qui l’a commandée, avant tout œuvre de mélancolie et d’« inquiétante étrangeté », mêlant pulsion du désir et pulsion de mort, merveilleux et cruauté, quotidienneté et invraisemblance, comme le faisait la poupée Olimpia du conte d’Hoffmann (_L’Homme au sable_, 1817) qui marqua tant Bellmer. Les surréalistes – Paul Eluard, André Breton, Henri Parisot et Georges Hugnet – ne s’y sont pas trompés, en appelant à eux, au vu de quelques photographies en noir et blanc de _La Poupée_ en cours de fabrication, cet artiste berlinois obscur qui venait de publier, à compte d’auteur à Karlsruhe, un recueil confidentiel et miniature intitulé _Die Puppe_. Ces photos, reproduites dans _Minotaure_ en 1935 (sous le titre _Poupée. Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée_) et dans _Cahiers d’art_ en 1936, présentes dans nombre d’expositions de groupe, sont les premières « prises de vue ». Ces images sont comme autant de « tableaux vivants » mettant en scène les infinies variations d’un corps improbable, et que Bellmer va bientôt colorier à l’aniline et au pinceau (voir au Musée les trois épreuves coloriées de 1949-1963 de la donation Daniel Cordier, AM 1989-219-221) pour en « hystériser » encore l’artifice et la séduction. Répondant aux nouveaux impératifs ambivalents de la « beauté convulsive » : « érotique-voilée, explosante-fixe, magique-circonstantielle », cette beauté est toute de contradictions actives. Artefact poétique, _La Poupée_ en appelle à l’imaginaire inconscient le plus secret.

Au-delà de son appartenance pleine au surréalisme (Paul Eluard lui consacre, en 1938, quatorze poèmes qui seront édités, avec les photographies coloriées, dans _Les Jeux de la Poupée_, en 1949), l’étrange objet progressivement articulé se prête, grâce à ce rouage parfait qu’est la « boule de ventre », à tous les possibles corporels – se dédoublant, se scindant, s’ouvrant, se fermant. Il nourrit le propos singulier, tout à la fois _expérimental_ et _théorique_, de l’« anatomie du désir », qui va être au centre de la recherche visionnaire d’un Bellmer humaniste-ingénieur. Une incroyable géographie interne du corps, compris comme une vaste anagramme d’inversions et de réversions, de remembrements et de démembrements, de coalescences et de contractions, de proliférations sans fin, est donnée à voir. La quête que l’artiste poursuit à partir de et avec _La Poupée_, est celle, vertigineuse, obsessionnelle, sadienne, d’une image par où « revitaliser » le désir et créer de nouveaux phantasmes. C’est un « monstrueux dictionnaire » des ambivalences corporelles qui est, avec elle, initié.

Agnès de la Beaumelle

Title

La demie poupée
===============

1971

Artist

[Hans Bellmer](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/artists/bellmer-hans/)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Germany, France

13 Mar 1902 – 23 Feb 1975

[![Image 1: Woman-like mannequin seated on wooden chair, adorned with tartan bow, black choker, pink bracelet, sock and shoe](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/media/thumbnails/collection_images/8/89.1996%23%23S.jpg.935x1200_q85.jpg)](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/media/collection_images/8/89.1996%23%23S.jpg "view larger image")

*   ### Details

Other Title The half doll Date 1971 Media category[Sculpture](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/?media=sculpture)Materials used wood, paint and assemblage Dimensions Doll: 90.0 cm (height) Signature & date

Artist information Hans Bellmer

[7](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/?artist_id=bellmer-hans)

Share[![Image 2: twitter](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/media/iconomizer/twitter_40x40_blue.svg)](https://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=La%20demie%20poup%C3%A9e%20-&url=http://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/89.1996/&via=ArtGalleryofNSW)[![Image 3: facebook](https://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/media/iconomizer/facebook_40x40_black.svg)](http://facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http://www.artgallery.nsw.gov.au/collection/works/89.1996/)  
*   ### About

Hans Bellmer’s influence straddles several generations. He became a member of the surrealist group in the early 1930s and continued drawing and creating sculptures into the 70s, including this work completed in 1971. The subject matter of his art can be traced back to his childhood, when he had erotic fantasies about his young cousin Ursula. Later he was to be greatly influenced by ‘The tales of Hofmann’,1 which revealed to him a world in which childhood and art were linked. Bellmer began making surrealist drawings and sculptures while he was still living in Germany although he was rarely able to show them, and in 1935 created 18 photographs for the surrealist magazine ‘Minotaure’. Fleeing the attention of the Nazis, he took up residence in France in 1938 but was interned along with Max Ernst until 1940. Even in France Bellmer’s work was beyond most public limits and found its place in the experimental publications and happenings organised by the surrealists. His themes were often highly erotic, exploring the inside and outside of the body, exaggerating genital areas and violently distorting the human form. A number of writers of the day included his images in their texts, including Paul Eluard and notably Georges Bataille, who commissioned Bellmer to provide illustrations for his influential book ‘Histoire de l’oeil’ (the story of the eye).

While in his drawings Bellmer was free to imagine all manner of contortions, his photographs depended on the poses he could contrive with his sculpted dolls, or poupées. These he constructed to allow a multitude of variations. His first version was more rigid; his second had a fully articulated body and included a spherical belly around which he could arrange up to four legs, four bulbous breasts, an upper torso, three pelvises, a pair of arms and the recycled head and hands of his first doll. It is this second version that most often features in his photography. By dressing the dolls in girls’ dresses with large ribbons in their hair and schoolgirls’ shoes, he added further variation. The figures could then be posed in bizarre situations on stairways and beds, or against trees, often as if in bondage.

‘La demie poupée’ is simpler in that it has only one leg, one arm and one breast. Like his earlier dolls, it wears an enormous bow at the back of its bald head, a white sock and ‘Mary-Jane’ shoe. Possibly, its most bizarre feature is its head, which is configured more like the head of a penis or the cleft of a buttock – only the small puckered mouth confirms that it is at least part human.2 These gender mutations are typical of Bellmer’s work but they also find contemporary resonance with the abject objects and images created by artists such as the Chapman brothers and Cindy Sherman, and aspects of works by Francesco Clemente and Dennis Del Favero.

1. Jacques Offenbach’s play ‘The tales of Hofmann’ directed in 1931–32 by Max Reinhardt. In the play the protagonist falls hopelessly in love with an automaton.

2. See Susan Best, ‘Just looking? The body, the gaze, and syncope’, in ‘Body’, AGNSW, Sydney 1997, p 89

14.title: Hans Bellmer, The Doll/La Poupée – Smarthistory
14.content:
![Image 1: copy url icon](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/themes/sh-new-theme/assets/images/copy-icon.svg)

![Image 2: page icon](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/themes/sh-new-theme/assets/images/page-icon.svg)

![Image 3: print icon](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/themes/sh-new-theme/assets/images/print-icon.svg)

![Image 4: quote icon](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/themes/sh-new-theme/assets/images/quote-icon.svg)

Jump To

The first time I encountered Hans Bellmer’s life-sized double-doll sculpture—at an exhibition I helped organize at the International Center of Photography in 2001—my feelings were a mix of shock, revulsion, and fascination. In _The Doll_ photo-series based on the sculpture, Hans Bellmer assembled and reassembled doll parts that he had constructed with his brother Fritz—also a trained engineer. Bellmer accentuated and duplicated their female sex organs, splaying them out on the floor as a still life before the viewer. Due to the nature of the work from this series, he is often pegged by scholars as a misogynist-leaning, female-objectifying artist—even to the extent of having alleged “pedophiliac” visual fantasies. [1] But Bellmer also provides a compelling example of the complexities of reading artwork retroactively. As scholars since the year 2000 have suggested with _The Doll_ and other photographs from the series, Bellmer also expressed his own gender-identity issues, engaged the alternative realities of [Surrealism](https://smarthistory.org/surrealism-origins-and-precursors/), and commented on Nazi Germany’s notions of the “perfect” versus the degenerate body.

Bellmer was born in German-speaking Silesia but had been exposed to French Surrealism on trips to mid-1920s Paris, where he met the Italian artist much beloved by the Surrealists, [Giorgio De Chirico](https://smarthistory.org/de-chirico-soothsayers-recompense/), who often used mannequins as subjects for his paintings. Surrealist preoccupations with the uncanny melded with numerous highly personal events once the Bellmer family moved to Berlin in 1931. Together, these inspired the artist to construct his first life-sized doll in 1933—the same year Hitler took over as German Chancellor—which he could use as a subject for experimental photography. [2] That was followed by a more complex second doll in 1935 which was composed of a central ball joint that allowed for more flexibility and various appendages to be attached. While that opened up the object for Bellmer and kindled his desire to create various associations of gender and identity, it concurrently led to accusations of purposeful violence done to the doll’s “body” through implied amputations and sexualization.

As Therese Lichtenstein explored in depth in her 2001 monograph _Behind Closed Doors: The Art of Hans Bellmer_, the convergence of three events between 1930–32 inspired him to construct the first doll. They included his mother sending him a box of his childhood toys—including broken dolls. He also had a Lolita-like fixation on his teenage cousin Ursula Naguschewski, newly arrived in Berlin where the Bellmer family had moved. And finally, he attended a local production of _The Tales of Hoffman_, a Jules Offenbach opera, where the first act centered on a “beautiful, lifelike doll Olympia.” [3]

[![Image 5: Hans Bellmer, "Poupée: Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée (Doll: Variations on the Montage of an Articulated Minor)," Minotaure, number 6 (December 1934)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Minotaur-870x585.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Minotaur.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, “Poupée: Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée (Doll: Variations on the Montage of an Articulated Minor),” _Minotaure_, number 6 (December 1934)

### The circulation of Bellmer’s _Dolls_

The artist took approximately 30 black-and-white photographs of the first doll, some of which were included in the 1934 book _Die Puppe_(_“Dolls_”)and which also appeared in the Surrealist publication _Minotaure_ in December of 1934. His cousin Ursula, then a Sorbonne student in Paris, had shown them to the Surrealist founder and poet André Breton at Bellmer’s request, and they caused “such a stir” that they were quickly published as the double-page spread above.

[![Image 6: Hans Bellmer, La Poupée, 1935, hand colored gelatin silver print, 29.2 x 27.3 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/handcolored-300x321.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/handcolored.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, _La Poupée_, 1935, hand colored gelatin silver print, 29.2 x 27.3 cm (private collection)

Parts of that doll were then incorporated into the more monumental second doll in 1935, which was the subject of more than 100 photographs, including the images that have become “textbook” Bellmer such as _The Doll_ (_La Poupée_, 1935). This image was hand-tinted in candy-colored pastels, lovingly applied by Bellmer—an unusual practice when black-and-white photography was accepted as the default—with the parts adhered to a chair-caning surface. [4]

In a way, it’s unfortunate that this image from the series has become one of the most widely disseminated examples of Bellmer’s work. As striking as it is, other images of the second doll speak more directly to the complexity of gender and political issues that the artist sorted out through these performative sculptural acts before photographing them, with the photographs then becoming his definitive works of art. A different photograph also entitled _The Doll_ (the repeated titles can become confounding) from 1936 shows how the ball joint of the more flexible second doll can be used to attach multiple legs.

[![Image 7: Hans Bellmer, The Doll, 1936, hand-colored gelatin silver print, printed 1949, 13.7 x 13.7 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bellmer-trousers-870x859.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Bellmer-trousers.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, _The Doll_, 1936, hand-colored gelatin silver print, printed 1949, 13.7 x 13.7 cm (private collection)

Bellmer therefore had more choices of garb here and chose to put one set of legs into men’s trousers and another set laid bare to show off girly patent-leather shoes. The artist was very forthcoming about his own lingering gender confusion, speculating that it may have been precipitated by his tyrannical, fascistic father who was obsessed with masculinity, underwhelmed by his sons’ lack of demonstration of it, and who eventually joined the Nazi Party. Bellmer described himself and his brother as children: “In fact, we were probably rather adorable, more like little girls than the formidable boys we would have preferred to be. Yet, it seemed to be more fitting than anything else to lure the brute out of his place in order to confuse him.” [5] And so it seems safe to presume that he often identified _himself_ directly with the doll.

### Rejecting Nazi “perfection”

One of the most astonishing experiments with the doll parts is witnessed through a 1936 _Doll_ photograph, a hand-colored photographic print depicting a torso where a second set of legs replace the arms and head and which is dressed in red and clad in two sets of the black leather shoes: the type typically worn by young girls. Concurrently in the forest setting, an ominous and voyeuristic figure dressed in all black hovers behind a nearby tree, ready to pounce, with all the implied features of a strongly-built male.

[![Image 8: Hans Bellmer, The Doll (La Poupée), 1936, hand-colored vintage gelatin silver print, 6 x 5.5 cm (private collection)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Red-trousers-870x867.jpg)](https://smarthistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Red-trousers.jpg)

Hans Bellmer, _The Doll (La Poupée)_, 1936, hand-colored vintage gelatin silver print, 6 x 5.5 cm (private collection)

Is this scene based on voyeuristic sexual fantasies? Or perhaps it refers to the suffocating environment of surveillance instituted by the Third Reich, a regime Bellmer protested, and as a result, refused to work or exhibit with publicly. He claimed _The Doll_ was a political artwork, but many viewers focused on the sexual content. Other hand-tinted images of the doll created a sense of diseased skin, which the art historian Therese Lichtenstein emphasizes was a protest against the desire for perfection in [Nazi](https://smarthistory.org/art-in-nazi-germany/) “body culture.” The persuasive combination of possibilities is precisely what complicates Bellmer’s arresting and disturbing works.

### Bellmer and Surrealism

The interwar Nazi politics of Germany became so constricting for Bellmer that when his sickly wife died in 1938, he moved to Paris where he lived for the rest of his life. He was immediately embraced by the Surrealists there who included him in the [_International Exhibition of Surrealism_](https://smarthistory.org/surrealist-exhibitions/) in 1938, with its famed “Street of Mannequins.” Surrealist poet Paul Eluard wrote poems to accompany Bellmer’s second doll’s photographs in the book _Games of the Doll_, although it was not published until 1949. In the late 1940s Bellmer also collaborated with the author Georges Bataille, providing illustrations for his 1947 reprint of the novella _Story of the Eye._

Later in his career, he began additional “body-art” collaborations with his lover, the German writer and artist Unica Zürn. However, Zürn suffered deeply from her mental health issues, and died in 1970. The following year he was able to enjoy a definitive retrospective at the Centre national d’art contemporain, Paris, including an overview of his dolls. He died a few years later and was laid to rest in the illustrious Père Lachaise Cemetery in his beloved adopted city, where the artistic movement of Surrealism had always welcomed him with open arms.

[1] Ken Johnson, “[Desiring Machines: Hans Bellmer and Surrealist Strategies in Contemporary Photography](https://www.nytimes.com/2002/05/03/arts/art-review-desiring-machines-hans-bellmer-surrealist-strategies-contemporary.html),” _New York Times_ (May 3, 2002). This review shows that those assumptions about Bellmer lingered even after the turn of the millennium.

[2] Freud’s essay regularly invoked dolls, mannequins, mirrors, and other doubles as examples of the “uncanny.” Sigmund Freud, “[The Uncanny](https://archive.org/details/freud-uncanny_001/mode/2up),” (1919), _The Standard Edition of the Complete Works of Sigmund Freud,_ volume 17, translated by James Strachey (London: The Hogarth Press, 1964), pp. 217–56.

[3] Therese Lichtenstein, _Behind Closed Doors: The Art of Hans Bellmer_ (Berkeley: University of California Press, 2001), p. 21.

[4] For an example of such a textbook, see Mary Warner Marien, _Photography: A Cultural History,_ 5 th edition (London: Laurence King Publishing, 2021), p. 253.

[5] Hans Bellmer, “Die Vater (The Father),” 1936, translated by Allen S. Weiss from the French, “Le Père,” which appeared as a prose poem in _Le Surréalism_, number 4 (Spring, 1958). See Lichtenstein, p. 177.

Hans Bellmer
============

In often violently erotic photographs and drawings, Hans Bellmer developed the Surrealist theme of mannequins and dolls as metaphors of sexuality with a singularly obsessive focus. He explored the usually pubescent female figure as fetish object. Bellmer's series _Die Puppe (The Doll)_, debuted in the 1934 issue of the Surrealist publication _Le Minotaure_, and the photographs were described as "variations on the assemblage of an articulated minor." The doll consisted of a wood-and-metal skeleton covered with a realistic body of plaster and papier mâché; a system of ball-joints allowed it to be shaped into endless disturbing configurations, appearing dismembered and monstrous.

Born in Katowice, Silesia, Bellmer worked in coal mines before entering the Berlin Technische Hochschule to study engineering in 1923. While there, he also studied perspective with George Grosz and established contact with Dada artists. From 1924 to 1936 he worked variously as a typographer and draftsman. He first made contact with the Surrealists in 1924 on a trip to Paris. In 1932 he was inspired by the opera _The Tales of Hoffmann_, and the next year collaborated on a production of Hoffmann's _The Sandman_: both works feature female automatons. At around this time, in opposition to the rise of Nazism, he stopped all work that supported the state. Bellmer began constructing his first "artificial girl" in 1934, with his wife, Margarete. Photographs of the doll were hand-colored by Bellmer for the first edition of his book _Die Puppe_. The second series of dolls, even more disarticulated than the first, were created in 1936-1938. Bellmer left Berlin in 1938 and settled in Paris where he was part of Surrealist circles. With the outbreak of the war, he was interned as a German citizen in a prison camp from 1940-1941. Bellmer's work appeared in numerous exhibitions, including the 1947 International Surrealist Exposition in Paris.

Lisa Soccio

6.title: (#137) Hans Bellmer
6.content:
Description
-----------

*   Hans Bellmer

*   SELF-PORTRAIT WITH DIE PUPPE
*   gelatin silver print

mounted, signed in red ink on the mount, inscribed ‘La Poupée, par Hans Bellmer’ and initialed by André Breton in red ink and stamped ‘27’ and ‘792’ on paper labels on the reverse, framed, National Gallery of Art, Washington, D. C., and Museum of Modern Art, New York, exhibition labels and an Ubu Gallery label on the reverse, 1934

Provenance
----------

The collection of André Breton, Paris

Calmels Cohen, Paris, _André Breton, 42, rue Fontaine_, 15 April 2003, Lot 5042

Acquired from Ubu Gallery, New York, 2004

Exhibited
---------

Paris, Musée national d’art modern/Centre Georges Pompidou, _André Breton, la beauté convulsive_, 1991

Washington, D. C., National Gallery of Art, _Foto: Modernity in Central Europe_, June - September 2007

New York, The Museum of Modern Art, _The Original Copy: Photography of Sculpture_, August - October 2010: and traveling to Kunsthaus Zürich, February - May 2011

Literature
----------

_Andre Breton, la beauté convulsive_ (Centre Georges Pompidou, 1991), p. 316 (this print)

_Foto: Modernity in Central Europe_(Washington, D. C.: National Gallery of Art, 2007), pl. 58 (this print)

_Die Puppe_ (Karlsruhe: Thomas Eckstein, 1934), pl. 3 (reversed)

_Minotaure,_ No. 6, Winter 1934, p. 30

Alain Jouffroy, _Bellmer_(William and Noma Copley Foundation, nd. [1961]), pl. 3 (reversed)

Peter Webb and Robert Short, _Hans Bellmer_ (London, 1985), pl. 34 (reversed)

Condition
---------

This print is on double-weight paper with a very glossy surface. It is essentially in excellent condition. The surface is sufficiently glossy to suggest that the print has been ferrotyped, but it lacks the uneven gloss or slightly "crazed" look that ferrotyped prints frequently have. The glossy surface accentuates the detail in the photograph, and the doll in particular is rendered with great, unsettling, clarity. When examined very closely in high raking light, some light scuffs can be seen on the print's surface; these are inconsequential and do not break the emulsion. The photograph has lifted very slightly from the mount in the upper corners and in one small spot on the top edge; this can only be seen upon close examination. The photograph is mounted to stiff board. A rectangular sheet of paper, smaller than the mount, has been affixed to the reverse of the mount, and Breton's notations, and the numerical stamps appear on this. On the reverse of the mount, and the top edge, is a thin strip of modern paper tape along the top edge. 

In response to your inquiry, we are pleased to provide you with a general report of the condition of the property described above. Since we are not professional conservators or restorers, we urge you to consult with a restorer or conservator of your choice who will be better able to provide a detailed, professional report. Prospective buyers should inspect each lot to satisfy themselves as to condition and must understand that any statement made by Sotheby's is merely a subjective qualified opinion.

**NOTWITHSTANDING THIS REPORT OR ANY DISCUSSIONS CONCERNING CONDITION OF A LOT, ALL LOTS ARE OFFERED AND SOLD "AS IS" IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE CONDITIONS OF SALE PRINTED IN THE CATALOGUE.**

Catalogue Note
--------------

This arresting and enigmatic Hans Bellmer self-portrait is from the series of photographs he made in 1933 and ’34, in Berlin, documenting the construction of his first Doll figure. Bellmer published this image in his 1934 book, _Die Puppe_, which included 10 sequentially-ordered photographs of the figure’s creation. Also in that year, he sent these photographs, through his cousin, to Paris, where they were shown to André Breton, from whose collection this print comes. Breton was immediately impressed, and with Paul Eluard, published a suite of 18 Bellmer photographs, including this self-portrait, in the Winter 1934 number of the Surrealist journal _Minotaure_, under the title ‘_Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée_’ (_‘Variations on the assemblage of an articulated minor’)._

Bellmer began work on the Doll in 1933, with the goal of ‘construct[ing] an artificial girl with anatomical possibilities which were capable of re-creating the heights of passion even to inventing new desires’ (quoted in Webb, p. 29). Infused with his own brand of high-concept eroticism, Bellmer had next to deal with the logistical challenge of creating a figure that would, in its appearance and articulation, meet his high standards. Working with his engineer brother, Fritz, Bellmer first constructed a wooden armature with hinged joints. This was slowly and carefully covered with flax fiber and plaster and shaped to resemble a human form, and then fitted with an eerily convincing plaster face. The photographs in _Die Puppe_ document the transition of the work from wooden ‘skeleton’ to the disconcertingly lifelike finished figure. Like the self-portrait, several images show preliminary designs for the Doll hung on the studio wall. In these photographs, the Doll is indisputably an artificial thing, yet it is close enough, in some of its aspects, to a living being that its appearance is truly uncanny. In the photograph offered here, for example, the Doll seems to react to Bellmer’s presence, and the viewer cannot help but project a narrative onto the image. It was part of Bellmer’s genius that he knew how to use photography not solely as a documentary device, but more importantly as a tool to infuse his creation with life.

Ultimately, Bellmer and his brother created a mannequin that was both a fascinating simulacrum and, surprisingly, a viewing device. As a way of imbuing the Doll with an inner life, Fritz conceived the idea of installing a ‘panorama’ within the Doll’s stomach. This circular device housed several painted scenes which could be viewed by peering through the Doll’s navel. The viewer advanced to the next scene by pressing a button on the Doll’s left nipple. In the present photograph, the compartment for the as-yet uninstalled panorama can be seen.

Although Bellmer officially joined the Surrealists in the 1930s, he conducted his earliest work with the Doll, and executed his photographs of it, in Berlin, in isolation from the movement. Yet the complete novelty of the Doll, and its exuberantly transgressive qualities, made it an object of fascination for the Surrealists. As Webb notes, ‘Looking for the first time at the photographs of Bellmer’s Doll, Breton, Eluard and their friends were confronted with the archetypal surrealist object. An ostensibly innocent toy had been snatched from the hallowed, protected domain of the nursery, enlarged to child size, and converted into a garish fetish that arouses the most ambiguous, unavowable, and palpably erotic desires. No surrealist object is more pregnant with riddles’ (Webb, p. 44).

This is the only image from this series of photographs in which Bellmer himself appears. While the artificial Doll is rendered here with solid clarity, the artist himself – who was in the frame for just a portion of the photograph’s total exposure time – is only half-present as a translucent, enigmatic form.

Detailed description
--------------------

| Artist | [Hans Bellmer](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/ressources/personne/cj77kGG) (1902, Allemagne - 1975, France) |
| --- |
| Main title | _La Poupée_ |
| Creation date | [1935 - 1936] |
| Place of production | Objet articulé (avec éléments de 1933-1934), additions et réfections en 1945 et 1970-1971 |
| Domain | [Objet](https://www.centrepompidou.fr/en/recherche/oeuvres?domaineCollection=Objet) |
| Techniques | Bois peint, papier mâché collé et peint, cheveux, chaussures, chaussettes |
| Dimensions | 61 x 170 x 51 cm |
| Acquisition | Don de l'artiste à l'Etat, 1972 Attribution, 1976 |
| Collection area | Arts Plastiques - Moderne |
| Inventory no. | AM 1976-927 |

Analysis
--------

Objet fétiche, placé au cœur d’une œuvre éminemment transgressive, essentiellement photographique et dessinée, la fameuse _Poupée_ grandeur nature de Hans Bellmer n’est pas loin d’être devenue une icône, ouvrant la voie à une réflexion très actuelle sur l’intégrité corporelle et l’identité sexuelle. De son temps, elle a œuvré comme une bombe, pulvérisant les catégories convenues : ni objet ni sculpture, elle se constitue en _organisme_ hybride, polymorphe, et en _instrument_ manipulable et transformable à l’infini. Et si elle peut être considérée comme un ultime avatar des mannequins, automates et robots produits en grande série dans l’Allemagne dévastée du tournant de la Grande Guerre, elle dépasse l’esprit de dérision et de satire sociale qui commandait cette vogue d’esprit dadaïste : à usage privé, répondant à une pulsion subjective (une nostalgie de l’enfance et de ses jeux, un abandon définitif à l’imagination érotique), elle est, au-delà de l’esprit de révolte contre l’ordre nazi qui l’a commandée, avant tout œuvre de mélancolie et d’« inquiétante étrangeté », mêlant pulsion du désir et pulsion de mort, merveilleux et cruauté, quotidienneté et invraisemblance, comme le faisait la poupée Olimpia du conte d’Hoffmann (_L’Homme au sable_, 1817) qui marqua tant Bellmer. Les surréalistes – Paul Eluard, André Breton, Henri Parisot et Georges Hugnet – ne s’y sont pas trompés, en appelant à eux, au vu de quelques photographies en noir et blanc de _La Poupée_ en cours de fabrication, cet artiste berlinois obscur qui venait de publier, à compte d’auteur à Karlsruhe, un recueil confidentiel et miniature intitulé _Die Puppe_. Ces photos, reproduites dans _Minotaure_ en 1935 (sous le titre _Poupée. Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée_) et dans _Cahiers d’art_ en 1936, présentes dans nombre d’expositions de groupe, sont les premières « prises de vue ». Ces images sont comme autant de « tableaux vivants » mettant en scène les infinies variations d’un corps improbable, et que Bellmer va bientôt colorier à l’aniline et au pinceau (voir au Musée les trois épreuves coloriées de 1949-1963 de la donation Daniel Cordier, AM 1989-219-221) pour en « hystériser » encore l’artifice et la séduction. Répondant aux nouveaux impératifs ambivalents de la « beauté convulsive » : « érotique-voilée, explosante-fixe, magique-circonstantielle », cette beauté est toute de contradictions actives. Artefact poétique, _La Poupée_ en appelle à l’imaginaire inconscient le plus secret.

Au-delà de son appartenance pleine au surréalisme (Paul Eluard lui consacre, en 1938, quatorze poèmes qui seront édités, avec les photographies coloriées, dans _Les Jeux de la Poupée_, en 1949), l’étrange objet progressivement articulé se prête, grâce à ce rouage parfait qu’est la « boule de ventre », à tous les possibles corporels – se dédoublant, se scindant, s’ouvrant, se fermant. Il nourrit le propos singulier, tout à la fois _expérimental_ et _théorique_, de l’« anatomie du désir », qui va être au centre de la recherche visionnaire d’un Bellmer humaniste-ingénieur. Une incroyable géographie interne du corps, compris comme une vaste anagramme d’inversions et de réversions, de remembrements et de démembrements, de coalescences et de contractions, de proliférations sans fin, est donnée à voir. La quête que l’artiste poursuit à partir de et avec _La Poupée_, est celle, vertigineuse, obsessionnelle, sadienne, d’une image par où « revitaliser » le désir et créer de nouveaux phantasmes. C’est un « monstrueux dictionnaire » des ambivalences corporelles qui est, avec elle, initié.

Agnès de la Beaumelle

7.title: The Erotic Imagination of Hans Bellmer
7.content:
![Image 1: Two women are kissing in an unfinished pencil sketch](https://www.rectoversoblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/47737_002-548x800.jpg)

Hans Bellmer was a Surrealist German artist and photographer. Born in 1902 and initially working in the fields of advertising and graphic design before transitioning to fine art, Bellmer’s first major project was also one of his best-known – _Die Puppe_, or a group of life-sized and sexualized pubescent female dolls.The goal of this first project was to oppose Nazi fascism by not creating anything that would support the Third Reich, which he attempted to achieve by criticizing and commenting on the cult of the perfect body which existed in the German state at the time.

![Image 2: Abstract human body sketch by an unknown artist, features multiple breasts, foot, penis, hand, and hair, all contained within a circle](https://www.rectoversoblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/47737_005-577x800.jpg)

He took inspiration for his doll project from a variety of places, including reading the published letters of Austrian poet and playwright Oskar Kokoschka and attending a performance of Jacques Offenbach’s Tales of Hoffman in which a man falls in love with an automaton. He began to physically construct his first doll in 1933, which stood approximately 56 inches tall. In 1934 Bellmer anonymously published a book,_The Doll (Die Puppe)_, which contained 10 black-and-white photographs of the doll arranged in a series of tableaux. Also in 1934, photographs of his doll appeared in the Surrealist journal _Minotaure_ with the title “Poupée: Variations sur le montage d’une mineure articulée”. The doll was shown in some cases with sexualized props including a black veil, lacy undergarments, or flowers, or in some photos simply as a pile of doll parts. Of the doll, Bellmer wrote, “It was worth all my obsessive efforts when, amid the smell of glue and wet plaster, the essence of all that is impressive would take shape and become a real object to be possessed.” (Bellmer, 1934)

![Image 3: A graphite pencil drawing of a female torso, nude, is from the chest down](https://www.rectoversoblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/47737_003-561x800.jpg)

Bellmer was eventually declared a degenerate artist and was forced to f lee Germany for France, where he was welcomed into the Surrealist circles there. He gave up doll-making but spent the rest of his life continuing to push sexual and erotic boundaries with a variety of explicit drawings, etchings, photographs, paintings, and prints of pubescent girls. F.A. Bernett currently has in its inventory an important work from this period of Bellmer’s creative life.

![Image 4: Female bodies are drawn in pencil](https://www.rectoversoblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/47737_001-568x800.jpg)

_À Sade_ comprises a portfolio of ten incredibly explicit and surrealistic erotic etchings inspired by and in homage to the Marquis de Sade, the famous French libertine best known for his pornographic writings which emphasize violence, suffering, and blasphemy. The etchings are remarkable examples of Bellmer’s obsessive and meticulous treatment of the body especially the female form – limbs, genitalia, eyes, breasts, and buttocks are distorted or conflated, combining desire and horror in a way typical of both Bellmer’s work and de Sade’s.

![Image 5: Abstract drawing is a surreal and intricate composition featuring human-like figures and organic forms](https://www.rectoversoblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2018/09/47737_004-589x800.jpg)

Bellmer, Hans. **À Sade.** Unpaginated portfolio including title page, colophon, and ten explicit and detailed etchings inspired by the erotic writings of the Marquis de Sade, most plates approx. 7 7/8″ x 5 7/8″, each printed on 15″ x 11 1/16″ sheet, housed in separate blank folder with guard sheet, all signed in pencil by the artist. Contents loose as issued, in wrpps. portfolio, laid into cloth folder and slipcase. N.p. 1961. No. 30 of an edition of 50. ([47737](https://www.fabernett.com/pages/books/47737/hans-bellmer/a-sade))

_Although published anonymously, our research shows that it was published in Paris by Alain Mazo. Incredibly scarce; as of April 2018, WorldCat locates only one copy in a German library and none in North America._
